---
title: "Mutually exclusive events"
---

Suppose that one observed token is either nominative or accusative under our four form pronoun representation. A single form cannot have both surface cases. We need to distinguish this structural fact about the events from any claim about how frequent the cases are.

Let

$$
N=\{\textit{he},\textit{they}\}
$$

be the nominative event and let

$$
A=\{\textit{him},\textit{them}\}
$$

be the accusative event. The two sets share no outcomes:

$$
N\cap A=\varnothing.
$$

Events whose intersection is empty are [**mutually exclusive**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html). They cannot both occur on one realization of the outcome represented by $\Omega$.

The definition concerns set membership:

$$
B\text{ and }C\text{ are mutually exclusive}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
B\cap C=\varnothing.
$$

No probability appears in this definition. We can establish mutual exclusivity before assigning any numerical mass.

## Add probabilities across exclusive events

Under the toy probability measure,

$$
\mathbb{P}(N)=.20+.10=.30
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{P}(A)=.30+.40=.70.
$$

Since $N$ and $A$ are mutually exclusive, their union contains two nonoverlapping parts. The probability measure thus gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(N\cup A)
&=\mathbb{P}(N)+\mathbb{P}(A)\\
&=.30+.70\\
&=1.
\end{aligned}
$$

In this representation, $N\cup A=\Omega_4$. The sum equals one because the two events are both exclusive and exhaustive.

Exclusivity and exhaustivity are separate properties. Consider the singleton events $\{\textit{he}\}$ and $\{\textit{them}\}$. They are mutually exclusive because they share no outcome. Their union does not equal $\Omega_4$, so their probabilities sum to $.20+.40=.60$, not to one.

## Work through a nonexclusive pair

Let

$$
P=\{\textit{they},\textit{them}\}
$$

be the plural event. Compare $P$ with the accusative event $A$. Their intersection is

$$
P\cap A=\{\textit{them}\}.
$$

The pair is not mutually exclusive because *them* makes both events occur. Directly adding $\mathbb{P}(P)=.50$ and $\mathbb{P}(A)=.70$ would count the mass on *them* twice. The result $1.20$ is a warning that the nonoverlap condition has failed.

The base R set check should come before the arithmetic.

```{r}
#| eval: false
nominative <- c("he", "they")
accusative <- c("him", "them")
plural <- c("they", "them")

length(intersect(nominative, accusative)) == 0
length(intersect(plural, accusative)) == 0
```

The first expression returns `TRUE`; the second returns `FALSE`.

## The represented outcome matters

Mutual exclusivity is always relative to what happens once. If one outcome is one pronoun token, nominative and accusative forms are mutually exclusive in the toy representation. If one outcome is a sentence containing two pronouns, the event “the sentence contains a nominative pronoun” and the event “the sentence contains an accusative pronoun” may occur together.

The linguistic labels have not changed. The unit represented by one outcome has changed, and that change alters the intersection.

## Labels do not guarantee mutual exclusivity

Contrasting linguistic labels do not by themselves imply an empty intersection. Terms such as *singular* and *plural* often denote mutually exclusive values of one annotation. But terms such as *plural* and *accusative* denote values on different dimensions and may overlap.

The safe procedure is to write the events as sets and compute their intersection. If the intersection is empty, the events are mutually exclusive under the declared sample space. The labels alone do not establish the result.

## Check your understanding

1. Are $\{\textit{he},\textit{him}\}$ and $\{\textit{they},\textit{them}\}$ mutually exclusive? Are they exhaustive?
2. Let $F$ be the first person event and $P$ the plural event in the larger pronoun sample space. Write $F\cap P$ and decide whether the events are mutually exclusive.
3. Give two mutually exclusive events that are not exhaustive in $\Omega_4$.
4. Explain why changing the outcome from one token to one sentence can change whether two linguistic events are mutually exclusive.

Mutual exclusivity tells us when two events cannot occur together. The [next page](joint-probability-of-events.qmd) assigns a probability to the event in which two properties do occur together.
